newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya sees marginal growth in sugar production.
newsitem.headline: Kenya sees marginal growth in sugar production.

text.p: Kenya's sugar output, held back by drought and illegal imports, will expand marginally to 400,000 tonnes in 1997 from 386,000 last year, officials said on Thursday.
"Drought has affected cane in main growing districts, which means we cannot expand as fast as we would like," an executive from the state Kenya Sugar Authority (KSA) told Reuters.
A drought that began in late November broke at the end of March.

"Imported sugar that has illegally found its way into the Kenyan market has also meant that there are high stocks held by sugar mills, which discourages them from improving their capacity," the executive added.
Consumption is forecast to rise to 600,000 tonnes in 1997 from 560,000 in 1995 and 1996.

Opening stocks in January were 24,113 tonnes and millers produced 42,211 tonnes in the month. Some 32,856 tonnes were sold in January, but stocks at the end of the month totalled 41,974 tonnes versus 50,243 a year earlier.

The KSA, whose figures for February and March were not available, said January's sharp rise in stocks reflected marketing problems. "The major factor contributing to this being the massive importation of sugar in 1996," it said in a review.

Officially, sugar imports totalled 65,826 tonnes in 1996 against 24,440 in 1995. But shipping sources said as much as 200,000 tonnes of sugar, mostly labelled as being for transhipment to neighbouring countries, ended up on the Kenyan market.

Kenya Ports Authority officials said Kenya imported 105,270 tonnes of sugar in the first quarter of the year but did not provide comparative figures for last year. But KSA figures show that only about 2,000 tonnes have been imported.
This week customs and tax authorities launched a crackdown on illegal imports by impounding thousands of tonnes of sugar labelled for transit but found stored privately.
Customs officials said they had seized sugar worth 110 million shillings found stored privately instead of at a government bonded warehouse.

Customs, Kenya Revenue Authority and Kenya Sugar Authority officials said they had also seized 250,000 100-kg bags of sugar in a warehouse. They suspected the sugar was originally labelled for transhipment but was offloaded into Kenya.
In retail outlets imported sugar is six percent cheaper than locally produced sugar.
